patient.name: Rukhsana Begum
patient.complaint: Worsening breathlessness, palpitations and coughing up streaks of blood
background: Grew up in Sylhet, Bangladesh; rheumatic fever aged 10
Moved to Tower Hamlets 20 years ago
Told of a 'heart murmur' at a GP check 5 years ago

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?' from the murmur: mid-diastolic rumble with opening snap (MS) vs pansystolic to the axilla (MR). Also post-MI acute MR and the cause of a lesion.

points: Rukhsana, 46: breathless walking to the bus stop for 6 months.
Two days of a **racing, irregular heartbeat**.
Coughing **blood-streaked sputum**; has to sleep on three pillows.
Voice has become **hoarse**; solid food sticks.

steps.lead: Rukhsana's symptoms come from a mitral valve that **obstructs** flow from left atrium to left ventricle.

points: **Rumbling mid-diastolic murmur** at the apex, best heard on her left side in expiration.

steps.q: Which valve lesion fits a mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap at the apex?
steps.r: **Mitral stenosis**: mid-diastolic rumble, opening snap, loud S1, best with the patient on the left side in expiration.

steps.lead: Rukhsana has the full MS picture: rheumatic fever, dyspnoea, haemoptysis, AF, malar flush, dysphagia and **Ortner's** hoarseness.

steps.text: Do not mix up the axilla and the carotids: pansystolic to the **axilla** is MR; ejection systolic to the **carotids** is aortic stenosis.

steps.lead: Rukhsana's problem is chronic. The emergency to recognise is **acute MR 2–10 days after an MI** from papillary muscle rupture.
Rukhsana's enlarged left atrium has tipped her into **AF**, and her orthopnoea and crackles point to pulmonary oedema.

visual.title: Rukhsana's ECG
visual.caption: Irregularly irregular, no P waves: **atrial fibrillation** from left atrial enlargement.

steps.text: A mitral valve patient who suddenly worsens has usually gone into **AF**: the loss of atrial kick plus a fast rate shortens diastolic filling time.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which investigation confirms the diagnosis?' (transthoracic echo), and 'most likely ECG or CXR finding' (AF; cardiomegaly and pulmonary oedema).

steps.q: What confirms Rukhsana's diagnosis and severity?
steps.r: **TTE** is the gold standard: it shows valve structure, the type of lesion and severity.

steps.lead: Rukhsana's **ECG shows AF**; her **CXR** shows an enlarged heart and pulmonary oedema.

visual.title: Rukhsana's chest X-ray
visual.caption: Enlarged cardiac silhouette (large left atrium) and pulmonary venous congestion.

steps.lead: Rukhsana's **TTE** shows thickened, fused leaflets with a small valve opening: rheumatic mitral stenosis.

steps.title: Rukhsana's echo and bloods
steps.text: Severe MS. Thyroid and potassium are normal, so the AF is from her valve.

visual.title: Mitral valve area
visual.label: Rukhsana 1.1
visual.caption: Below 1.5 cm² is severe: she needs an intervention, not just tablets.

steps.text: ECG and CXR support the diagnosis but cannot confirm it. The answer to 'confirm' or 'gold standard' is **echocardiography**.

management.exam: Expect watch-and-wait for asymptomatic MS, furosemide and rate control for symptoms, PBMV for severe MS, repair for severe MR and emergency surgery for acute post-MI MR.

points: Furosemide IV for her pulmonary oedema; crackles settle.
Anticoagulation started for AF with mitral stenosis.

steps.lead: Rukhsana is **symptomatic**, so tablets ease her: **furosemide** for fluid, a **beta-blocker** for AF rate, anticoagulation for stroke risk.

steps.text: AF with moderate-severe **mitral stenosis** is anticoagulated with **warfarin** (UK/ESC practice), not a DOAC.

visual.title: Rukhsana's heart rate on bisoprolol
visual.caption: Slower rate = longer diastole = more time to fill through the narrow valve.

steps.q: Rukhsana has severe MS with a pliable valve and no clot. What is the definitive treatment?
steps.r: **PBMV** splits the fused commissures through a catheter. Repair is the preferred operation for **MR**, not MS.

steps.lead: Rukhsana is listed for **balloon valvuloplasty**. If her valve were heavily calcified, she would need open valve replacement.
**PBMV** (percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty) is the first choice for Rukhsana's severe, pliable rheumatic MS.

steps.title: Mitral stenosis pathway
nodes: Asymptomatic: watch and wait, review 6 months, echo 6–12 months
Symptomatic: furosemide; beta-blocker and anticoagulation if AF
Severe: PBMV, or open valve replacement
steps.caption: Severity and symptoms decide.

steps.lead: If Rukhsana had **acute MR** from papillary muscle rupture after an MI, the answer would be **emergency** valve surgery.

steps.text: Acute post-MI MR with pulmonary oedema and shock is not a diuretic-and-wait case: it is an **emergency surgical referral**.

science.exam: Expect applied mechanism questions: molecular mimicry in rheumatic fever, why MS causes haemoptysis and AF, and why papillary muscle rupture is so dangerous.

steps.lead: Rukhsana's childhood **strep throat** triggered rheumatic fever: antibodies attacked her valve and fused the commissures.

steps.title: From strep throat to mitral stenosis
nodes: Molecular mimicry: antibodies cross-react with valve tissue

steps.lead: The narrow valve backs pressure into Rukhsana's left atrium and lungs: **dyspnoea**, **haemoptysis** and AF.
Years of stretch have disrupted the electrical pathways in Rukhsana's enlarged atrium, setting up **AF**.

steps.q: Why did Rukhsana's AF make her breathless so quickly?
o: Lost atrial kick and short diastole reduce LV filling
steps.r: MS already limits filling. **Losing atrial contraction** and a **fast rate** (short diastole) cut filling further, so LA and lung pressures rise.

steps.lead: In MR, the LA and LV are **volume overloaded** each beat: LA dilation gives AF and LV dilation leads to failure.
**Posteromedial** papillary muscle rupture after an inferior MI floods unprepared lungs: sudden pulmonary oedema and shock.

o: Early diastolic at left sternal edge
mcq.r: **Mid-diastolic rumble with an opening snap** at the apex, left lateral, expiration.
**Pansystolic at the apex radiating to the axilla**, louder on expiration.

o: Hoarseness from LA compressing recurrent laryngeal nerve
Malar flush from low cardiac output
mcq.r: An enlarged **left atrium** compresses the **recurrent laryngeal nerve**.

What is the gold-standard investigation for mitral valve disease?
What is the minimally invasive definitive treatment for severe MS?

o: Review in 6 months, echo every 6–12 months

mcq.q: Which drug helps LV dysfunction in chronic MR?
mcq.r: **ACE inhibitors** (ramipril, enalapril) for LV dysfunction in MR.

mcq.q: Which complication do chronic MS and MR share?
mcq.r: Both dilate and strain the **left atrium**, causing **AF**.

points.p: Pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla

Acute breathlessness in chronic disease = acute pulmonary oedema

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: echo confirms; ECG and CXR support.
Exam thinking: symptoms and severity decide.

points.why: No medication if no heart failure.
Symptom relief if unfit for surgery.

points.p: AF: beta-blocker rate control and anticoagulation
Severe: PBMV or open mitral valve replacement

prompts.tip: Exam thinking: tablets for symptoms, repair for severe, emergency for acute.

Acute post-MI MR: emergency repair or replacement

prompts.q: Why does rheumatic fever cause mitral stenosis?

points.why: Antibodies to group A strep hit valve tissue.

points.p: Fibrosis, calcification and commissural fusion narrow the orifice

prompts.q: Why does MS cause haemoptysis and AF, and MR cause heart failure?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: follow the pressure and volume.

points.p: MS obstructs LV filling, raising LA pressure
Back pressure into pulmonary circulation gives dyspnoea and haemoptysis
MR volume-overloads LA and LV; LV dilation gives heart failure
Papillary muscle rupture: acute severe MR, sudden pulmonary oedema, shock (no time to adapt)

glossary.Mitral stenosis: Narrowing of the mitral valve, obstructing flow from left atrium to left ventricle.
glossary.Mitral regurgitation: Backflow of blood from the left ventricle into the left atrium during systole.
glossary.Rheumatic fever: Autoimmune illness after group A streptococcal throat infection that can scar heart valves.
glossary.Rheumatic heart disease: Long-term valve damage, mainly mitral, caused by rheumatic fever.
glossary.Opening snap: A sharp early-diastolic sound as stiff mitral leaflets snap open in mitral stenosis.
glossary.Mid-diastolic murmur: A murmur in the middle of diastole, such as the rumble of mitral stenosis.
glossary.Pansystolic murmur: A murmur lasting all of systole, as in mitral regurgitation.
glossary.Malar flush: Plum-red cheeks seen in mitral stenosis from low cardiac output.
glossary.Ortner's syndrome: Hoarse voice from an enlarged left atrium compressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.
glossary.Recurrent laryngeal nerve: Branch of the vagus nerve that supplies the vocal cords.
glossary.AF: Atrial fibrillation: chaotic atrial activity giving an irregularly irregular pulse.
glossary.Atrial fibrillation: Chaotic atrial electrical activity with an irregularly irregular ventricular rate.
glossary.Papillary muscle: Muscle in the ventricle that anchors the mitral leaflets via chordae.
glossary.Papillary muscle rupture: Tear of a papillary muscle after MI, causing sudden severe mitral regurgitation.
glossary.Posteromedial papillary muscle: Mitral papillary muscle usually supplied only by the RCA, so it ruptures after inferior MI.
glossary.Commissure: The junction where two valve leaflets meet.
glossary.Commissural fusion: Leaflets stuck together at their edges, narrowing the valve; typical of rheumatic MS.
glossary.Molecular mimicry: Antibodies against a microbe cross-react with similar host proteins.
glossary.PBMV: Percutaneous balloon mitral valvuloplasty: a catheter balloon splits the fused commissures.
glossary.Balloon valvuloplasty: Widening a narrowed valve by inflating a balloon across it through a catheter.
glossary.Mitral valve repair: Surgery that fixes the patient's own mitral valve; preferred over replacement for MR.
glossary.TTE: Transthoracic echocardiography: ultrasound of the heart through the chest wall.
glossary.Echocardiography: Ultrasound imaging of the heart showing valves, chambers and blood flow.
glossary.Furosemide: Loop diuretic used to clear fluid in heart failure and pulmonary oedema.
glossary.ACE inhibitor: Drug such as ramipril that lowers afterload and protects a failing left ventricle.
glossary.Bisoprolol: Beta-blocker used for rate control in AF.
glossary.Warfarin: Vitamin K antagonist anticoagulant; used for AF with moderate-severe mitral stenosis.
glossary.Anticoagulation: Drugs that reduce blood clotting to prevent stroke in AF.
glossary.Pulmonary oedema: Fluid in the lung air spaces from high pulmonary venous pressure.
glossary.Cardiomegaly: An enlarged heart shadow on chest X-ray.
glossary.Atrial kick: The extra ventricular filling from atrial contraction, lost in AF.
glossary.Degenerative mitral valve disease: Wear-and-tear or myxomatous change of the mitral valve; the commonest UK cause of MR.
glossary.Mitral valve prolapse: Floppy mitral leaflets bulging back into the left atrium in systole.
glossary.Loud P2: Loud pulmonary component of the second heart sound, suggesting pulmonary hypertension.

technique.stem: A 71 year old man has 9 months of increasing breathlessness and fatigue. He has never had a myocardial infarction. His pulse rate is 82 bpm regular and BP 134/78 mmHg. The apex beat is displaced. There is a pansystolic murmur loudest at the apex radiating to the axilla, louder in expiration.
technique.q: Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?

steps.x: Valve abnormality from a murmur: timing, site, radiation, manoeuvre.
Pansystolic + apex + axilla = MR. Displaced apex = volume-loaded LV. Expiration favours left-sided lesions.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mitral regurgitation**, most likely degenerative in a UK 71 year old.

elim: AR is early diastolic at the left sternal edge.
AS is ejection systolic to the carotids.
MS is mid-diastolic with an opening snap.
TR is at the lower left sternal edge and louder on inspiration.

steps.x: **C. Mitral regurgitation.** Pansystolic to the axilla.

technique.stem: A 52 year old woman who had rheumatic fever as a child has increasing breathlessness. She has a malar flush, a loud first heart sound and a mid-diastolic murmur at the apex. Her pulse rate is 76 bpm regular and BP 122/74 mmHg. Her ECG shows sinus rhythm with a broad, notched P wave.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?

steps.x: Confirm the diagnosis: what is the gold standard for valve disease?
Clinical MS; the notched P wave (P mitrale) shows LA enlargement.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transthoracic echo** confirms MS and grades severity.

elim: Catheterisation is invasive and not first to confirm valve disease.
Cardiac MRI is not first-line for valves.
CXR may show a big LA but cannot confirm MS.
CT angiography looks at coronary arteries.

steps.x: **E. TTE.** ECG and CXR support; echo confirms.

technique.stem: A 79 year old woman has rheumatic mitral stenosis with ankle swelling and breathlessness on minimal exertion. She is in sinus rhythm. She has severe COPD and is judged unfit for valve intervention. Her pulse rate is 78 bpm, BP 124/70 mmHg. There are bibasal crackles and pitting ankle oedema.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate management of her symptoms?

steps.x: Symptom management in MS when intervention is not an option.
Symptomatic fluid overload, no AF, no intervention possible.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Oral furosemide** for symptomatic relief.

elim: No arrhythmia to treat.
Digoxin is for AF rate control; she is in sinus rhythm.
She has been judged unfit for valve intervention.
ACE inhibitors are for LV dysfunction in MR; they can drop BP in fixed MS obstruction.

steps.x: **C. Oral furosemide.** Diuretic for fluid; beta-blocker only if AF.

technique.stem: A 44 year old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops palpitations. Her pulse is irregularly irregular at 136 bpm. Echo shows a mitral valve area of 1.2 cm² and a markedly dilated left atrium.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her arrhythmia?

steps.x: Mechanism of an arrhythmia in MS.
AF in a patient with a big left atrium from severe MS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Raised LA pressure dilates the atrium; **stretch disrupts conduction**, causing AF.

elim: An accessory pathway is WPW, not MS.
SA node ischaemia gives bradycardia, not AF here.
MS obstructs inflow; afterload is not the issue.
No thyroid features; the valve explains it.

steps.x: **B.** Big left atrium = AF.

practice.stem: A 38 year old woman who grew up in Nigeria has 6 months of breathlessness on exertion and recent haemoptysis. She has a malar flush. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm regular and BP 116/72 mmHg. There is a loud first heart sound, an opening snap and a low-pitched rumbling murmur at the apex in mid-diastole, heard best with her lying on her left side.
practice.q: Which is the most likely heart valve abnormality?
practice.e: Opening snap and mid-diastolic rumble at the apex with malar flush and haemoptysis is mitral stenosis, usually rheumatic. Tricuspid stenosis is at the lower sternal edge and louder on inspiration.

steps.x: Valve abnormality from the murmur.

clues: rumbling murmur at the apex in mid-diastole
steps.x: Diastolic rumble + opening snap + apex = MS. Haemoptysis from pulmonary venous hypertension.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Mitral stenosis.**

elim: AR is early diastolic at the left sternal edge.
AS is ejection systolic to the carotids.
MR is pansystolic to the axilla.
TS is at the lower sternal edge, louder on inspiration.

steps.x: **D. Mitral stenosis.** Snap + rumble + apex.

practice.stem: A 49 year old woman with known mitral stenosis has a 2 month history of a hoarse voice. She does not smoke. Her pulse rate is 96 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 118/70 mmHg. Laryngoscopy shows a paralysed left vocal cord. Echo shows severe mitral stenosis with a massively dilated left atrium.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her hoarse voice?
o: Compression of the left recurrent laryngeal nerve by the left atrium
practice.e: Hoarseness in MS from a large left atrium compressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve is Ortner's syndrome.

steps.x: Cause of a symptom in a patient with known MS.
Left cord palsy + giant LA in MS.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Ortner's syndrome**: LA compressing the left recurrent laryngeal nerve.

elim: Laryngoscopy shows palsy, not a tumour, and she does not smoke.
Reflux causes irritation, not cord paralysis.
No neck swelling is described.
Nodules come from voice overuse and do not paralyse the cord.

steps.x: **A.** MS + hoarse = Ortner's.

practice.stem: A 66 year old man had an inferior myocardial infarction 4 days ago. He suddenly becomes very breathless. His pulse rate is 122 bpm, BP 84/52 mmHg, respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 85% breathing air. There is a new pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla, and crackles to the mid zones.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Acute mitral regurgitation from papillary muscle rupture
practice.e: Sudden pulmonary oedema and shock 2–10 days after an inferior MI with a new apical pansystolic murmur to the axilla is papillary muscle rupture. A VSD murmur is at the left sternal edge.

steps.x: Diagnosis of a post-MI deterioration.

clues: new pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla
steps.x: Day 4, inferior MI (posteromedial papillary muscle, RCA), apical murmur to axilla, flash pulmonary oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute MR from papillary muscle rupture.**

elim: Tamponade gives muffled sounds and raised JVP, not a new murmur.
Dressler's is pericarditis weeks after MI.
An aneurysm gives persistent ST elevation, weeks later.
VSR murmur is at the lower left sternal edge, often with a thrill.

steps.x: **A.** Days post-MI + apical murmur to axilla + pulmonary oedema = papillary rupture.

practice.stem: A 58 year old woman with rheumatic mitral stenosis has had 6 hours of severe breathlessness and pink frothy sputum after starting to feel her heart racing. Her pulse rate is 148 bpm irregularly irregular, BP 104/66 mmHg, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 87% breathing air. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: In chronic MS, new fast AF shortens diastolic filling and causes acute pulmonary oedema, with pink frothy sputum and bilateral oedema on CXR.

steps.x: Diagnosis of acute breathlessness in a patient with chronic MS.
Chronic MS + new fast AF + pink frothy sputum + bilateral oedema.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Acute pulmonary oedema** (triggered by AF).

elim: Asthma gives wheeze, not frothy sputum or cardiomegaly.
Pneumonia gives fever and focal consolidation.
Pneumothorax shows a lung edge, not bilateral oedema.
PE gives a clear CXR.

steps.x: **B.** Chronic mitral disease + acute breathlessness = acute pulmonary oedema.

practice.stem: A 51 year old woman who moved from India 10 years ago has increasing breathlessness. Echo shows thickened mitral leaflets with commissural fusion and a valve area of 1.3 cm². Her pulse rate is 84 bpm and BP 120/74 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her valve disease?
practice.e: Commissural fusion with stenosis in a woman from a high-prevalence country is rheumatic heart disease, the commonest cause of MS.

steps.x: Cause of the valve lesion.
Mitral stenosis with commissural fusion; endemic background.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Rheumatic heart disease.**

elim: Congenital MS presents in childhood.
Annular calcification is in the elderly and spares the commissures.
Endocarditis destroys valves, causing regurgitation.
Lupus gives Libman-Sacks vegetations, rarely stenosis.

steps.x: **D.** MS = rheumatic until proven otherwise.

practice.stem: A 76 year old man in London has 2 years of slowly increasing breathlessness. He has no fever, no history of rheumatic fever and no previous myocardial infarction. His pulse rate is 78 bpm regular and BP 138/82 mmHg. There is a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his murmur?
practice.e: In the UK, degenerative disease is the commonest cause of mitral regurgitation. No fever, no MI and no rheumatic history make the others unlikely.

steps.x: Cause of a murmur: MR, then why.
Chronic MR in an older UK man with no infective, ischaemic or rheumatic story.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Degenerative mitral valve disease.**

elim: No fever; IE is subacute or acute, not 2 years.
No MI and the onset is not sudden.
Rheumatic disease mainly causes MS and needs a history.
VSD is at the left sternal edge, usually from childhood.

steps.x: **A.** UK MR = degenerative.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with known moderate mitral regurgitation has had palpitations for 3 days. Her pulse rate is 118 bpm irregularly irregular and BP 128/80 mmHg. She is not breathless at rest.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on her ECG?
o: Delta waves with a short PR interval
practice.e: Chronic MR dilates the left atrium and predisposes to atrial fibrillation: an irregularly irregular pulse with no P waves.

steps.x: Most likely ECG finding in a mitral patient.
Mitral disease + irregularly irregular pulse.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Atrial fibrillation.**

elim: Delta waves are WPW, unrelated to MR.
LBBB gives a regular pulse.
Mobitz II is regular with dropped beats, usually slow.
No chest pain to suggest STEMI.

steps.x: **A.** Mitral disease + irregular pulse = AF.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man has a pansystolic murmur at the apex radiating to the axilla and increasing breathlessness. His pulse rate is 80 bpm, BP 132/76 mmHg. His ECG shows sinus rhythm. Chest X-ray shows mild cardiomegaly.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis and assess severity?
practice.e: Transthoracic echocardiography is the gold standard for mitral valve disease, showing structure, regurgitation and severity.

steps.x: Confirm and grade the lesion.
Suspected MR; ECG and CXR already done.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Transthoracic echocardiography.**

elim: Invasive and not needed to confirm MR.
Exercise testing is for ischaemia, not to diagnose valve disease.
Repeating the X-ray adds nothing.
BNP suggests heart failure but cannot show the valve.

steps.x: **E. TTE** confirms and grades.

practice.stem: A 42 year old woman has a mid-diastolic murmur found at a routine check. Echo shows mild-moderate rheumatic mitral stenosis with a valve area of 1.8 cm². She has no symptoms and no signs of heart failure. Her pulse rate is 72 bpm regular, BP 118/72 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Review in 6 months with echocardiography every 6–12 months
practice.e: Asymptomatic MS without heart failure needs no medication: watch and wait with review in 6 months and echo every 6–12 months.

steps.x: Management of MS without symptoms.
Asymptomatic, not severe, sinus rhythm.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Watch and wait** with regular review and echo.

elim: Replacement is for severe disease.
No fluid overload to treat.
PBMV is for severe stenosis.
No AF, so no anticoagulation.

steps.x: **D.** No symptoms = watch and wait.

practice.stem: A 47 year old woman has severe symptomatic rheumatic mitral stenosis. Echo shows a valve area of 0.9 cm² with pliable, non-calcified leaflets, mild mitral regurgitation and no left atrial thrombus. Her pulse rate is 82 bpm, BP 116/70 mmHg. She is otherwise fit.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
practice.e: Severe MS with a pliable valve, no thrombus and little MR is ideal for PBMV, which splits the fused commissures. Repair is the operation of choice for MR.

steps.x: Definitive treatment for severe MS.
Favourable valve anatomy for a balloon.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **PBMV.**

elim: Repair is preferred for severe MR, not MS.
Diuretics only relieve symptoms.
ACE inhibitors are for LV dysfunction in MR.
TAVI treats aortic stenosis.

steps.x: **C. PBMV.** Calcified valve or thrombus = open replacement instead.

practice.stem: A 70 year old man had an inferior myocardial infarction 5 days ago. He develops sudden severe breathlessness. His pulse rate is 128 bpm, BP 82/50 mmHg and oxygen saturation 84% breathing air. Echo shows a flail posterior mitral leaflet with severe mitral regurgitation from a ruptured papillary muscle.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate definitive management?
o: Emergency mitral valve repair or replacement
practice.e: Acute MR from papillary muscle rupture needs emergency mitral valve repair or replacement. Medical therapy only stabilises him for surgery.

steps.x: Definitive management of a mechanical post-MI complication.
Cardiogenic shock from acute severe MR.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Emergency surgery**: valve repair or replacement.

elim: An ACE inhibitor in shock would drop BP further.
PBMV opens a stenosed valve; this one leaks.
Waiting a week risks death.
Thrombolysis treats occluded arteries, not a torn muscle.

steps.x: **A.** Papillary muscle rupture = emergency surgery.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has mitral stenosis. She had a sore throat followed by fever, painful migrating joints and a rash at the age of 9. Echo shows thickened leaflets with fused commissures.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her valve damage?
o: Direct streptococcal infection of the valve
Immune complex deposition on the valve
Molecular mimicry between streptococcal antigens and valve tissue
practice.e: In rheumatic fever, antibodies to group A streptococcal antigens cross-react with valve proteins (molecular mimicry), causing fibrosis and commissural fusion.

steps.x: Mechanism of rheumatic valve damage.
Rheumatic fever in childhood, MS decades later.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Molecular mimicry** causing autoimmune valvulitis.

elim: The valve is not infected; that is endocarditis.
Immune complexes cause Osler's nodes in IE.
Myxomatous change causes prolapse and MR.
Septic emboli are a feature of endocarditis.

steps.x: **C.** Rheumatic = molecular mimicry.
